Subject: Private deployment throughput & contingency planning

Hi Jonas / Marissa —

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. MiraHealth is moving fast on the protected VPC deployment and we need a short, actionable plan for throughput targets + what happens in a surge. High level asks:

- Our baseline is ~150 concurrent chat sessions sustained during working hours (avg seq len ~350 tokens). Peak loads (seasonal health drives) could be 3x baseline for short windows.
- We need a deterministic failover behavior: prefer graceful degradation (reduce model size / quantize, rate-limit non-critical endpoints) rather than full outage.
- What slack should we reserve in our initial committed pool to cover short spikes without falling back to hosted?

I attached our traffic spreadsheet for the next 6 months. Can you sketch preferred targets, a surge-handling flow, and any quick runbook items we should hand to ops?

Appreciate it — Tom

Attachments: mira_throughput_model_v1.xlsx (spreadsheet)

From: jonas_weber@redwood.com

Cc: laura_bennett@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 2 Nov 2026 09:18:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Private deployment throughput & contingency planning

Tom —

Thanks for the spreadsheet, that helps. Quick, high-level proposal so you have something to act on today:

1) Target sizing for initial commit
- Baseline: size pool for 160 concurrent sessions (10% buffer over your stated 150) on the plan to serve avg 350-token sequences with 95th pct latency < 300ms for chat-turn responses.
- Headroom: reserve an additional 40% burst capacity (hot standby nodes) that can be brought into the pool within 90s using our private autoscaling handshake. This handles short 2–5 minute spikes without model fallback.

2) Surge strategy & graceful degradation
- Preferred path: prefix-KV cache warm + dynamic quantized fallback: when queued requests > target_queue (see runbook) we immediately route new non-critical traffic to a quantized model variant (4-bit) with a conservative penalty on quality but much higher throughput.
- Secondary path: for > 2x sustained load beyond burst window, apply throttles per-account and degrade non-essential features (e.g., long-context embeddings, background reranking).
- Failover: only if all above fail do we route to hosted failover with strict rate limits and full audit logging.

3) Quick ops handoff items
- Configure autoscaler thresholds: CPU/GPU utilization 70% trigger, 85% hard scale; queue length threshold = 250 pending tokens; cold-start cap = 5 nodes.
- KV cache warmup: run warmup script after any scale event and on deploy; warm key prefixes for common prompts.
- Observability: per-route token rate and per-GPU tail latency metric at 99th pct. Alerting at 99.9th latency and sustained queue > 300 for 3m.

I attached a short guideline PDF and the warmup script. Happy to refine numbers with Aditya and Laura for procurement/commit sizing.

— Jonas
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Attachments: redwood-scaling-guidelines.pdf, kv-cache-warmup-script.sh

Subject: Re: Private deployment throughput & contingency planning — infra runbook

Team / Tom (cc'd for visibility) —

I've validated Jonas's numbers against our load model and Mira's spreadsheet; here are concrete infra configs and playbook steps that ops can follow. I'm keeping them terse so they can be copy/pasted into your internal runbook.

1) Node sizing & commit guidance
- Starting commit: 16 x A100-80GB equiv (gpus appear as "rwi-prod-" nodes). This maps to ~160 concurrent chat sessions at 350 tokens avg under our standard batching + 4-bit quantized fallback.
- Burst pool: keep 6 hot-standby nodes (same SKU) in off-state with a warmup image preloaded. These flip to active via a prioritized provisioning channel (expected readiness 60–90s).

2) Autoscaler & queue parameters
- Scale-up trigger: GPU util > 70% OR pending_queue_tokens > 200 for 30s. Scale-up increment: +2 nodes.
- Scale-down trigger: GPU util < 40% AND pending_queue_tokens < 40 for 3m. Cooldown: 5m.
- Max rollback window: 10m — if scale events exceed 4 in 30m consider increasing headroom.

3) Request routing & degradation ladder
- Normal: route to primary model (FP16 / near-full precision).
- Tier1 degrade: route to quantized model variant (Q4_0) for new sessions when pending_queue_tokens > 250. Keep prefix cache warmed for top-20 prompts.
- Tier2 degrade: throttle background jobs and force short-context summaries; notify product with preformatted alert "POOL_DEGRADE_TIER2".
- Tier3 failover: route non-PHI traffic to hosted fallback with rate cap; PHI-heavy requests should queue and alert for manual review.

4) Cache warmup & KV management
- On scale-up: run kv-cache-warmup-script.sh with top-keyset_1 for 90s. Warmup should prepopulate top 500 keys.
- Eviction policy: LRU with per-prefix caps to prevent cache thrash during burst.

5) Observability & SLOs
- Metrics to publish: per-gpu tail latency (p95/p99), pending_queue_tokens, per-route token rate, cache hit-rate.
- Alerts: p99 latency > 700ms for 2m; pending_queue_tokens > 300 for 3m; warmup failures.

6) Runbook play steps (incident quick win list)
- Step 0: Identify whether spike is organic or DoS via ingress IP distribution and auth-success rate.
- Step 1: Trigger burst pool manually if autoscaler lagging.
- Step 2: Flip new-session routing to Q4_0 variant (single command) and incrementally throttle long-context endpoints.
- Step 3: If still degraded after 10m, enable hosted failover and escalate to SE on-call.

Notes: keep a 15% commit cushion if Mira expects unpredictable marketing campaigns. For predictable seasonal blasts we can provision a scheduled warm window (pre-provision 30m prior).

If this looks good I can produce a one-page ops checklist for your runbook and a sample terraform snippet for the burst pool.

— Aditya Rao
Infra Reliability Lead
Redwood Inference
